Ran a small study on today's Brazil gap-downs: what drove them, which bounced, and how to decide which gaps are worth buying. 24 largest US-listed Brazilian names, full session incl. pre/post market. What happened: • Avg gap to the low: -26% (cap-weighted) • Bounce off the low: +12.8% • Only 39% of the gap won back by the last print • 4/24 filled intraday: $JBS $EMBJ $SUZ $GGB What explains it: how much revenue each company earns in Brazil. • Gap size: R² 0.48. ->Every +10pp of Brazil revenue = ~2.7pp more downside. ->Exporters fell ~4%, pure domestic names ~30%. • The bounce itself: R² 0.06. ->No link to Brazil exposure. Names bounced in proportion to how far they fell. • Whether the bounce held: R² 0.66. ->Exporters kept ~86% of their gap back. ->Domestic names kept ~25%. Exporters dragged down with the country (dollar earners, weaker real helps them) were collateral damage. Those gaps filled. Domestic names got a real repricing. The bounce was tradeable, but treating it as a gap fill was wrong. Overall this trade offers a hold as well, this is the exact same president we had in the past, yields, oil, a strong dollar and alike are actually turning into backwinds.

I agree that funded accounts can provide opportunities for traders with limited capital. That’s a legitimate benefit. But there’s a huge difference between accepting losses as part of trading and building a strategy around repeatedly blowing up accounts. When blowing up 20, 30, or 50 accounts becomes a normal part of pursuing payouts, what habits are we teaching aspiring traders? The goal should be to develop skills that compound over a trading career: risk management, discipline, consistency, and a repeatable edge.
